error_modes.label: WINGMAN ANTICIPATION OF NO1 INTENTION WITHOUT ASSUMPTION

texts.0: SP, due to a mental model of the flight built on assumption instead of on the briefed contract, acted on what No1 was expected to do rather than on what No1 actually did. SP initiated a position change for a turn that had never been signalled and left the briefed position with no visual signal or radio call received. The resulting geometry produced an uncontrolled closure with lead and the IP took control to separate the aircraft. The remaining formation profile was terminated.
texts.1: SP, due to a mental model that filled the gaps with assumption rather than with confirmed information, repeatedly started position changes before No1 signal was identified. Each wrong anticipation was corrected only after direct verbal prompting by the IP. Position and spacing were restored late and the flight was reformed at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete check of No1 visual signals against the briefed sequence, began to anticipate the next maneuver on expectation rather than on a confirmed signal. SP recognized the error before the deviation developed, returned to the briefed position and held it until the signal was given. No IP input was required and formation geometry stayed clear of the standard limits.
texts.3: SP anticipated No1 intention from the briefed sequence, the flight profile and lead aircraft attitude, but acted only on a confirmed visual signal or radio call. Position changes were initiated at the correct point, and where the picture was ambiguous SP asked instead of assuming.
texts.4: SP stayed one step ahead of No1 throughout the sortie, correlating the briefed sequence, lead energy state and the visual signals so that every position change was prepared before it was ordered. No action was taken on assumption at any point and each ambiguity was resolved with a short standard call. Formation integrity was maintained without a single unrequested movement.
texts.marginal: SP anticipated No1 intention correctly and generally acted on confirmed signals, but twice started the movement on expectation and verified the signal only afterwards. The trend was toward assuming rather than confirming whenever the sequence felt familiar. SP is expected to keep the anticipation mental and to move only after the signal has been positively identified.

error_modes.label: AWARENESS AND JUDGMENT - ORIENTATION AND CROSS-CHECK WHILE FLYING POSITION

texts.0: SP, due to a cross-check that stopped alternating between lead aircraft, own control and performance instruments and the outside references, lost track of the flight position relative to the field and the assigned area. Own altitude, airspeed and fuel state were left unmonitored while attention stayed on lead. The flight left the assigned area and descended through the briefed floor, and the IP took control to reposition and re-orient the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a slow and interrupted cross-check between lead aircraft and own instruments, did not keep track of what was happening in own aircraft while flying position. Orientation with respect to the field, the area boundary and the other flight members was re-established only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. The corrections were applied late and the resulting excursions reached the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that narrowed onto lead aircraft during the maneuvering, delayed the detection of developing altitude and fuel trends in own aircraft. SP recognized the omission without prompting, restored the alternation between lead, the instruments and the outside references and re-established orientation with respect to the field and the assigned area. The deviation stayed short of the standard limit and required no IP input.
texts.3: SP correlated continuously what was happening on the ground, in own aircraft and in the other flight members, alternating the scan between lead, the control and performance instruments and the outside references. Orientation with respect to the field, the assigned area and the traffic remained accurate, and the mission impact of each event was handled as it appeared.
texts.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted alternation between lead aircraft, own instruments and the outside references and continuously correlated flight position, fuel state and traffic. Adverse factors such as weather, airspace restrictions and traffic density were identified early and their effect on the formation was minimized before it degraded the mission. Orientation was never in doubt at any point of the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP kept orientation and stayed within the required standards, but the scan narrowed onto lead aircraft each time position keeping became demanding, and own instruments were checked only after the position was stabilized. The trend was toward monitoring lead at the expense of own aircraft state. SP is expected to keep own control and performance instruments inside the scan while flying position.

error_modes.label: RISK MANAGEMENT AND DECISION MAKING WITHIN THE FLIGHT

texts.0: SP, due to a failure to identify the contingencies of the formation profile before committing to it, continued the sortie into a hazard that had already been recognized by the flight. Available data on weather, traffic and fuel were not gathered before the decision, no alternative was considered and no decision was stated to the flight. The aircraft was flown into a position from which the hazard could no longer be avoided by the wingman alone and the IP intervened to break out the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete gathering of the available data, identified the hazard late and did not state a clear decision or its rationale to the flight. The alternative course of action was adopted only after the IP prompted it verbally and repeated the prompt. The hazard was avoided, but the margin achieved was at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial assessment based on partial information, delayed the decision to alter the profile after the hazard appeared. SP then gathered the missing data, identified the alternative, stated the decision to the flight with its rationale and regulated the flight path accordingly. The hazard was avoided in good time and without any IP input.
texts.3: SP identified contingencies and alternatives accurately, gathered the available data before deciding, stated the decisions clearly to the flight and gave the rationale when asked. Actual and potential hazards were recognized and the flight path was regulated so that they were positively avoided.
texts.4: SP identified the contingencies of each phase before they became relevant and had the alternatives ready with their decision points already defined. Decisions were stated to the flight early, concisely and with a rationale that lead could act on immediately. Every hazard was avoided by a wide margin with no degradation of the briefed profile.
texts.marginal: SP identified the hazards and reached correct decisions, but the decisions were formed late and were stated to the flight without the supporting rationale. The trend was toward deciding once the hazard was established rather than at the planned decision point. SP is expected to define the alternatives in advance and to state both the decision and its reason to the flight.

error_modes.label: TASK PRIORITIZATION AND SATURATION UNDER FORMATION WORKLOAD

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on holding the fingertip picture, dropped every other task while the workload increased. Radio calls, checks and the fuel check were omitted, and the tasks that were attempted were carried out in an order that violated the briefed sequence. Channelized attention on lead wingtip left the aircraft state unmonitored until the IP took control and re-established the flight.
texts.1: SP, due to attention captured by position keeping, handled the tasks one at a time and left the remainder pending as the workload built up. Missing radio calls and checks were completed only after the IP prompted each of them individually. The sequence was recovered late and the accumulated task backlog brought the sortie to the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on the position picture during the rejoin, delayed the secondary tasks and let two of them accumulate. SP recognized the developing saturation without prompting, re-ordered the tasks by significance and cleared the backlog before the next event. No task was ultimately dropped and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP put the tasks in order of significance without missing anything and without violating any rule, and handled multiple tasks in sequence while flying position. Task management remained deliberate as the workload increased and at no point developed into channelized attention on a single item.
texts.4: SP sequenced the flying, the checks, the radio and the visual scan so that each task was completed at its most efficient point and nothing accumulated. Task loading was distributed ahead of the busy phases, leaving spare capacity available at the rejoin and in the recovery. Attention was never captured by any single item, including the position picture itself.
texts.marginal: SP completed all the tasks in the correct order and inside the standards, but the ordering was reactive and secondary tasks were deferred each time position keeping demanded attention. The trend was toward a backlog that had to be cleared in the quiet phases. SP is expected to sequence the tasks ahead of the busy phases and to keep capacity in reserve for the rejoin.

error_modes.label: FLEXIBILITY AND CAPACITY - MISSION ADJUSTMENT AND USE OF AVAILABLE RESOURCES

texts.0: SP, due to a lack of assertiveness in stating unable when the flight profile exceeded own capability, continued to accept maneuvers that could no longer be flown safely in position. No alternative course of action was selected to reduce task loading, no knock-it-off was called and the remaining fuel and area were not taken into account. The aircraft was flown beyond SP capacity to control it in formation and the IP took control.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to state a limitation to the flight, adjusted the mission only after the IP directed it verbally. The remaining flight time, fuel and assigned area were not used efficiently and the profile was reorganized late in the sortie. Mission effectiveness was preserved only at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation in requesting a reduction of the profile as the conditions changed, continued at a task loading that was close to own capacity. SP then assessed the factors correctly, selected an alternative course of action and stated it to the flight in time, adjusting the remaining events to the available fuel and area. Mission effectiveness was maintained with no IP input.
texts.3: SP coped with the changing conditions of the sortie and adjusted the profile as needed to obtain the briefed objectives, remaining aware of how much task loading could be accepted safely. The remaining flight time, fuel and assigned area were used efficiently, and an alternative course of action was selected whenever it reduced the task loading.
texts.4: SP recognized the change of conditions before it affected the flight and reorganized the remaining profile so that the objectives were obtained within the available fuel, time and area. Own capacity was managed with a clear margin, and limitations and requests were stated to the flight early and without hesitation. No event was flown at the edge of SP capability.
texts.marginal: SP adjusted the mission correctly and never exceeded own capability, but the alternatives were selected late and the limitations were voiced only once the workload had already peaked. The trend was toward absorbing the task loading rather than reducing it. SP is expected to state the limitation and select the alternative at the point it is recognized, not after it becomes pressing.

error_modes.label: FLIGHT DISCIPLINE, CHECKS AND SOP COMPLIANCE

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete knowledge of the rules and procedures governing the formation sortie, did not carry out the operational checks in accordance with the checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. Required steps were performed out of order and briefed restrictions of the flight were exceeded. Recovery to base was not managed by SP and the IP took control and completed the procedures and the return to the field.
texts.1: SP, due to a superficial knowledge of the applicable procedures, performed the checks incompletely and out of the published order. Each omission was identified and corrected only after the IP prompted it, and the recovery was flown under continuous IP direction. The procedures were eventually completed, but at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption of the checklist flow while holding position, omitted one step of an operational check and delayed a briefed procedure. SP detected the omission without prompting, restarted the check from the correct point and completed the sequence in the published order. The recovery to base was flown correctly and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs, and carried out the required steps of each procedure in the proper order. Rules and briefed restrictions were respected throughout and the return to base was managed with minimum IP supervision.
texts.4: SP applied the checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs precisely and in the correct order at every phase, integrating them with the position keeping without any interruption of the flow. Knowledge of the rules and of the briefed restrictions was complete and applied without hesitation. The recovery to base was planned and executed independently, with no IP supervision required.
texts.marginal: SP completed all the checks and followed the published procedures, but items were occasionally performed out of the normal order and one check was started later than the planned point. The trend was toward fitting the procedures around the position keeping rather than planning them into the sequence. SP is expected to protect the checklist flow and to run each procedure at its briefed point.

error_modes.label: AGSM AS A CONTINUUM - STRAIN ONSET, INTENSITY AND BREATHING CYCLE

texts.0: SP, due to an anti-G straining maneuver started after the onset of G forces instead of before it, entered the high-G rejoin with no strain established and then held the strain for more than 3 seconds without breathing. Gray out developed at about 4 Gs and SP did not return to 1 G flight to reapply the strain. The IP took control, unloaded the aircraft and terminated all high-G maneuvering for the remainder of the sortie.
texts.1: SP, due to a strain applied at a fixed intensity rather than increased as the G increased, lost the leg, abdomen and chest contraction each time the loading built past 3 Gs. The IP had to call for the strain and for the breathing cycle before every high-G maneuver. Vision degraded briefly on two occasions and the required strain was produced only after verbal direction, leaving the AGSM at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a breathing cycle stretched beyond the 2 to 3 second interval during the first high-G turn, allowed the strain to become a single long hold. SP recognized the loss of G tolerance, returned to 1 G flight, reapplied the strain and re-entered the maneuver with full muscle contraction and constant breathing cycles. No vision degradation followed and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP started the AGSM before the onset of G forces and maintained it throughout the period of increased G loading, contracting legs, abdomen and chest and increasing the intensity of the strain as the G increased. Breathing was maintained at approximately every 2 to 3 seconds and no strain was held longer than 3 seconds without breathing. The lower-G segments were flown with all elements of the full AGSM at reduced intensity.
texts.4: SP treated the AGSM as a continuum for the whole sortie, setting the strain before every G onset and modulating its intensity with the loading without any break in the breathing cycle. Full muscle contraction and constant breathing cycles were held through the highest loadings of the profile, and the lower-G segments still received every element of the maneuver. No vision symptom of any degree occurred at any point.
texts.marginal: SP maintained an effective AGSM within the required standard, but the strain was set at the same intensity for every maneuver and the breathing cycle lengthened toward the end of each high-G turn. The trend was toward a fixed strain rather than one that follows the G continuum. SP is expected to increase the intensity of the strain with the loading and to keep breathing at approximately every 2 to 3 seconds.

error_modes.label: G-AWARENESS EXERCISE - PREREQUISITE, ENTRY PARAMETERS AND ONSET RATE

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the G-awareness exercise before a profile that included maneuvers requiring three or more Gs, went straight to high-G formation work with no evaluation of AGSM effectiveness or of personal G tolerance. Entry airspeed and deconfliction for the exercise were never briefed and sun angle and position were not considered before the first turn. The IP terminated the profile, took control and flew the exercise before any further maneuvering was allowed.
texts.1: SP, due to an entry flown below the 200 to 220 KIAS planning minimum and with the nose well outside 10 degrees of the horizon, could not sustain 4 Gs and let the exercise degrade into a descending spiral. The IP had to direct the power setting, the entry airspeed and the G onset rate step by step. The exercise was completed only after repeated verbal correction and met the acceptable standard by a small margin.
texts.2: SP, due to a G onset rate applied too rapidly on the first attempt, reached the target G before the effectiveness of the strain could be evaluated. SP recognized this, returned to 1 G flight, re-established maximum power and approximately 210 KIAS with the nose within 10 degrees of the horizon, and repeated the exercise with a slow and smooth onset. Approximately 4 Gs were then held for 4 to 5 breathing cycles without IP input.
texts.3: SP performed the G-awareness exercise before any maneuver that could require three or more Gs, entering a level to slightly descending turn at maximum power with sufficient airspeed to sustain 4 Gs and the nose within 10 degrees of the horizon. G onset was slow and smooth and approximately 4 Gs were maintained for approximately 4 to 5 breathing cycles to allow full cardiovascular response. Deconfliction was briefed and sufficient visual cues were confirmed available before the turn.
texts.4: SP planned and flew the G-awareness exercise to the 4 to 5 G band required for formation training, with entry airspeed, maximum power and nose position set precisely before the onset. The onset rate was deliberately slow so that the effectiveness of the strain could be assessed at each G increment, and the target was held for a full 4 to 5 breathing cycles. Sun angle, visual cues and deconfliction were addressed in the brief and confirmed in the air before the exercise was started.
texts.marginal: SP completed the G-awareness exercise within the required parameters, but entry airspeed was at the lower edge of the planning figure and the G was held for barely 4 breathing cycles. The trend was toward treating the exercise as a formality before the real maneuvering rather than as an assessment of the strain and of personal G tolerance. SP is expected to set the entry parameters with margin and to hold approximately 4 Gs for the full cardiovascular response.

error_modes.label: PROP WASH AND WAKE TURBULENCE - UNLOAD TO 1-G, EXIT AND G-METER CHECK

texts.0: SP, due to maneuvering behind No1 with no caution for the prop wash and wake turbulence in lead six o'clock, flew into the disturbed air with the aircraft loaded and continued to pull. SP did not unload to approximately 1-G, did not exit the area of turbulence and did not check the G-meter afterwards. The IP took control, unloaded the aircraft and terminated maneuvering, and a controllability check was carried out after the G-meter showed the aircraft limit exceeded.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed recognition of lead wake turbulence, remained in the disturbed air under load until the IP called for the unload. The unload to approximately 1-G, the exit from the turbulence and the G-meter check were each accomplished only after direct verbal direction. The G-meter reading stayed within limits, but the response was late enough to leave the recovery at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a lead pursuit correction that carried the aircraft toward lead six o'clock, entered prop wash while still loaded. SP recognized the encounter immediately, unloaded to approximately 1-G, exited the area of turbulence and checked the G-meter before reporting the reading to No1. Loading stayed inside aircraft limits and the exercise continued without IP input.
texts.3: SP maneuvered behind No1 with caution for the areas of prop wash and wake turbulence, particularly in lead six o'clock. On the single encounter SP unloaded to approximately 1-G, exited the disturbed air and checked the G-meter, reporting the reading at the next fuel and G-check. No G limitation was approached at any point of the exercise.
texts.4: SP anticipated the areas of prop wash and wake turbulence from lead flight path and geometry and positioned to avoid the six o'clock region before it developed. The one brief encounter was met with an immediate unload to approximately 1-G and a clean exit, and the G-meter was checked and reported without prompting. Loading remained well inside aircraft and personal limits throughout the exercise.
texts.marginal: SP handled the wake turbulence encounters within limits, but the unload was applied only after the aircraft had already been shaken and the G-meter was checked at the end of the set rather than immediately. The trend was toward reacting to the turbulence instead of predicting where lead disturbed air would be. SP is expected to unload to approximately 1-G on contact, exit the area and check the G-meter at once.

error_modes.label: JOKER AND BINGO FUEL DISCIPLINE WITHIN THE FLIGHT

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the increased frequency of fuel checks required during high fuel flow operations such as extended trail and low altitude work, did not notice the aircraft passing joker fuel. No1 was never informed and maneuvering continued well below joker with no reference to the briefed fuel plan. The IP made the fuel call to No1, directed the termination of the exercise and managed the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to fuel checks left at the normal interval through the extended trail exercise, reached joker fuel without recognizing it and made the call to No1 only after the IP prompted it. The fuel state was thereafter referenced from joker as required, but every subsequent check had to be initiated by the IP. The recovery was started in time by a small margin only.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held by position keeping during the low altitude segment, let two fuel checks pass unmade. SP recognized the omission, resumed the increased check frequency for the high fuel flow segment and informed No1 on reaching joker with the standard call. The remaining profile was flown against the revised fuel plan without IP input.
texts.3: SP performed regular fuel checks throughout the sortie and increased their frequency during the extended trail and low altitude segments and when approaching joker and bingo. No1 was informed on reaching joker fuel and the call was acknowledged, and the factors and assumptions behind the briefed joker and bingo were understood and applied. Recovery was initiated before bingo fuel as planned.
texts.4: SP tracked the fuel state continuously against the briefed joker and bingo, anticipating the high fuel flow segments and tightening the check interval before they began. The joker call to No1 was made at the exact point and carried the information lead needed to adjust the profile. Fuel remained ahead of the plan through the recovery and the arrival fuel matched the briefed figure.
texts.marginal: SP made the required fuel checks and the joker call inside the standard, but the checks were run at a fixed interval with no increase for the extended trail segment and the joker call followed the actual crossing by several seconds. The trend was toward reporting the fuel state rather than managing it. SP is expected to increase the check frequency during high fuel flow operations and to call joker at the point it is reached.

error_modes.label: NO2 PRIORITY ORDER - DECONFLICTION AND VISUAL BEFORE BACKING UP NO1
error_modes.source: technique:9.3 RESPONSIBILITIES - FLIGHT LEADER, NUMBER 1 AND NUMBER 2

texts.0: SP, due to inverting the No2 priority order and working on backing up No1 with navigation and radio while the geometry was closing, gave up flight path deconfliction and lost sight of lead during the rejoin. Position and clearing were both abandoned while SP wrote down a frequency change. The IP took control to deconflict the flight paths and to re-establish visual contact with No1.
texts.1: SP, due to crosschecking clearing and backing up lead at the expense of the first two priorities, allowed the position to deteriorate and briefly lost the visual picture of No1. The IP had to call for the reprioritization and for the blind call before SP acted on either. Deconfliction was preserved, but only through IP direction, leaving the performance at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to attention drawn to backing up No1 on the area entry, let the flight path deconfliction task slip while re-reading the navigation plan. SP recognized the inversion, reprioritized in the published order, re-established the position and only then resumed backing up lead. Separation from No1 stayed comfortable and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP applied the No2 priorities in the published order throughout the sortie, keeping flight path deconfliction from No1 first, the visual on lead second and being in position and on frequency third. Clearing for the formation and backing up No1 were performed as capacity allowed and never at the expense of the higher priorities. All of lead aircraft was used as reference rather than a single spot.
texts.4: SP held the No2 priority order without visible effort, so that deconfliction and the visual on lead were never in question even in the busiest phases of the profile. Clearing and backing up No1 were still accomplished in full, including a correct frequency and a timely position reference offered to lead. Whenever the workload rose SP shed the lower priorities first and picked them up again once the position was stable.
texts.marginal: SP kept the priorities in the correct order and remained inside the standards, but each time backing up No1 was required the position picture degraded before it was recovered. The trend was toward accepting the lower priority tasks in full regardless of what the geometry demanded. SP is expected to shed backing up lead first and to return to it once deconfliction and position are secure.

error_modes.label: TERMINATE, KNOCK IT OFF AND UNABLE - TIMELINESS OF THE CALL

texts.0: SP, due to waiting for the situation to develop instead of calling Knock It Off before the excursion, watched aspect, closure and line of sight rate build until the fighting wing cone was left and the 3/9 line was threatened. SP had also accepted a directed task beyond his ability without informing No1 and made no call at any stage. The IP called Knock It Off, took control and separated the aircraft from lead.
texts.1: SP, due to a reluctance to make the Terminate call while still apparently able to correct, delayed it until the position had already gone outside the cone parameters. The call was made only after the IP directed it, and the same delay was repeated on the following set. Deconfliction was maintained, but the timeliness of the calls stayed at the lower limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to persisting with a lead pursuit correction that was not arresting the closure, allowed the geometry to approach the bubble before recognizing that the position could not be regained. SP then called Terminate without hesitation, unloaded and rejoined at the next lower level of the exercise. The call was early enough to prevent any excursion and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP called Terminate or Knock It Off whenever the position could no longer be maintained or an unsafe situation was developing, and did so before the excursion rather than after it. Tasks directed beyond current ability were reported to No1 immediately and any doubt over the assigned position was resolved by an immediate query. No unsafe or unauthorized situation was allowed to continue unchallenged.
texts.4: SP made the Terminate and Knock It Off calls at the earliest point at which the trend was recognizable, so that each set ended with wide separation and no excursion. SP informed No1 clearly when a directed task exceeded present capability and queried at once whenever the assigned position was in doubt, with no hesitation over rank or role. The calls were standard, concise and always preceded rather than followed the problem.
texts.marginal: SP made the required Terminate and Knock It Off calls and no excursion resulted, but each call came after one further attempt to salvage the position rather than at the point the trend became clear. The trend was toward calling once the problem was established instead of before it. SP is expected to make the call as soon as the situation is evident, accepting that an early call is preferable to a late one.

error_modes.label: DYNAMIC FLYING SAFETY - CLEARING, SYSTEMS MONITORING AND PRE-PLANNED EMERGENCY RECOVERY

texts.0: SP, due to no emergency recovery plan established before the emergency occurred, had no field, heading or altitude in mind when a caution appeared during the area work. The distraction absorbed SP completely in a critical phase of flight, the airspace was not cleared and a converging aircraft went unseen. The IP took control, cleared the flight path, ran the required actions and set up the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to an emergency recovery plan that was never updated after the flight left the initial area, could state neither the nearest suitable field nor the fuel required when asked. Clearing and systems monitoring stopped for the duration of the simulated malfunction and resumed only after IP prompting. The plan was reconstructed with continuous IP assistance and remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to attention captured by an unexpected caution during the rejoin, interrupted the visual scan and left the airspace uncleared for several seconds. SP recognized the distraction, resumed clearing and systems monitoring and re-stated the recovery field and heading before continuing. Aircraft state and flight path were never in doubt and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP maintained an aggressive disposition toward gaining and maintaining situational awareness, clearing the airspace and monitoring aircraft systems continuously through the dynamic phases. An emergency recovery plan was established before it was needed and was updated as the flight moved between areas. The unexpected caution was handled without allowing it to distract from the critical phase of flight in progress.
texts.4: SP forecast and executed tasks from a continuous perception of self and aircraft in relation to the environment, the traffic and the mission, so that clearing and systems monitoring never lapsed. The emergency recovery plan was stated at every area change and included field, heading, altitude and fuel. When the unexpected caution appeared it was handled with no interruption of the flight path or of the visual scan.
texts.marginal: SP cleared the airspace, monitored the systems and had a recovery plan available, all inside the standards, but the plan was the one briefed on the ground and was not revised as the flight moved downrange. The trend was toward a static plan and a scan that narrowed whenever something unexpected appeared. SP is expected to update the emergency recovery plan with the flight position and to protect the clearing scan during distractions.
